1959 DeSoto Seville Is Not a Cadillac, but an Ultra-Rare Spring Special Mopar
13 photos
Photo: Charles Phoenix/YouTube
Seville is the capital of the autonomous region of Andalusia in southern Spain. To us car gearheads, it's also an iconic nameplate used by Cadillac between 1975 and 2004. But what if I told you that DeSoto also sold a vehicle sporting the Seville badge?
Don't worry if you haven't heard about it; it was a very short-lived model. And the fact that DeSoto hasn't been around for decades doesn't help either. In fact, I'd better refresh your memory before moving forward with this unknown model.
Named after Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto, the marque was established by Walter Chrysler in August 1928. It was founded three years after Walter created the Chrysler Corporation and introduced it alongside the Plymouth division. Both DeSoto and Plymouth were part of Chrysler's plan to divide its vehicle offering by price class.
Plymouth became the entry-level product, while DeSoto slotted between the latter and Dodge, which Chrysler purchased in 1928. DeSoto's initial role was to compete against carmakers like Studebaker, Hudson, and Pontiac in the mid-price class. In 1933, DeSoto was repositioned above Dodge and given access to some Chrysler body styles .
DeSoto went on to produce a version of the pioneering Airflow in 1933 and introduced the first mass-produced American car with pop-up headlamps in 1942. In the 1950s, it debuted the Adventurer, a limited-production, high-performance model similar to the exclusive Chrysler 300 letter series.
The division was phased out in late 1960, mainly due to low sales and overlapping with Chrysler's then-new and lower-priced Newport.
As for the Seville model you probably never knew existed, it was offered in 1959 as a Spring Special model. What's that, you ask? Well, it was common at the time for carmakers to offer mid-year promotional packages to boost dealership traffic and sales during the peak spring car-buying season. The Seville was a package that included various features. It was available on both the Firesweep and Firedome series .
This car is based on the Firesweep, which debuted in 1957 as an entry-level model. The Seville bundle included distinct exterior color configurations, a checkered upholstery pattern, and extra premium appointments such as a padded dashboard and color-keyed steering wheel. It also added "Seville" badges on the rear fenders.
The Seville you see here has a white over light blue exterior and a checkered interior in three-tone turquoise/gray, with darker turquoise stripes and white vinyl. And the really big deal here is that it's been restored to factory specifications and looks downright stunning inside and out.
The engine bay is just as gorgeous and houses the original 361-cubic-inch (5.9-liter) V8 engine. The mill was originally rated at 295 horsepower and 390 pound-feet (529 Nm) of torque and mated with Chrysler's popular three-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission.
In addition to being a spectacular sight, this DeSoto is also super rare. The company didn't keep records on Spring Special models, but experts say that the bundle found its way on only a tiny fraction of the Firesweeps built that year (due to its short-lived availability).
DeSoto produced 20,834 Firesweeps in 1969, and only 5,481 examples were two-door hardtops like the car you see here. Our host says that "only 2 or 3 are known to exist," and we might be looking at the finest one out there. Check it out in the video below.
